problem.text: Let $S$ be a set of $6$ integers taken from $\{1,2,\dots,12\}$ with the property that if $a$ and $b$ are elements of $S$ with $a<b$, then $b$ is not a multiple of $a$. What is the least possible value of an element of $S$?

steps.title: Where to start: group the numbers into chains
steps.body:
The rule forbids two elements where one divides the other. So sort $1$ to $12$ into chains in which each number divides every later one. Then $S$ can take at most one number from each chain.
$$\{1,2,4,8\},\ \{3,6,12\},\ \{5,10\},\ \{7\},\ \{9\},\ \{11\}$$

your_turn.prompt: Why can $S$ not contain two numbers from the chain $\{1,2,4,8\}$?
your_turn.answer: Any two of them have the smaller one dividing the larger one, which the rule forbids.

steps.title: Six chains, six elements
steps.body: There are exactly $6$ chains and $S$ has $6$ elements, so $S$ takes exactly one number from each chain. The chains $\{7\}$, $\{9\}$ and $\{11\}$ have only one choice, so $7$, $9$ and $11$ must be in $S$.

your_turn.answer: No. $1$ divides every other number, so it would clash with $7$, for example.

steps.title: The forced 9 knocks out 3
steps.body: Careful: it is easy to overlook that $9$ is forced. Since $9$ is in $S$ and $9$ is a multiple of $3$, the number $3$ cannot be in $S$. So from the chain $\{3,6,12\}$, $S$ must take one of the other two numbers.

your_turn.prompt: Which numbers can $S$ take from the chain $\{3,6,12\}$, and what do they have in common?

steps.title: Put it together
steps.body: Whichever of $6$ or $12$ is in $S$ is a multiple of $2$, so $2$ is out too. With $1$, $2$ and $3$ all ruled out, every element is at least $4$. The set $\{4,5,6,7,9,11\}$ works (no element divides another), so $4$ really happens. The answer is **(C)**.

wrong_choices.A: $2$ comes from starting with the primes $\{2,3,5,7,11\}$ and assuming a sixth number can be added. No sixth number fits, and in fact no valid $6$-element set can contain $2$.
wrong_choices.B: $3$ comes from missing that $9$ is forced into $S$. Once $9$ is in, $3$ cannot be, because $9$ is a multiple of $3$.
wrong_choices.E: $7$ comes from stopping at the easy set $\{7,8,9,10,11,12\}$. It works, but the question asks for the least value possible over all such sets.
